newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia opposition chiefs start election campaigns.
newsitem.headline: Croatia opposition chiefs start election campaigns.

text.p: Two opposition candidates who will challenge Croatian President Franjo Tudjman on June 15 began their campaigns on Wednesday, saying they were fighting against all the odds to offer a new vision for the future.

Unlike the nationalist president, whose daily schedule is meticulously covered by state media and whose campaign was boosted by a lavish birthday celebration carried live by state television, the challengers chose a low-profile approach.

Vlado Gotovac, a joint candidate of his Social Liberals and eight other centrist parties, kick-started his campaign at a news conference in the European House in Zagreb, under the motto "The Best Man for Croatia".

"Being an (opposition) presidential candidate in the cirumstances which hinder fair competition...can be described as 'jump and swim regardless of everything' -- that is against any hope," the poet and former dissident Gotovac said.

"But there is an important reason why we are putting up resistance in these circumstances -- this is a resistance against Croatia's undemocratic development, totalitarianism and degradation of public morality," he said.
"We want to reverse the direction of Croatia's social and economic life, and return to Croatia what was promised to it at the very beginning."
Zdravko Tomac of the Social Democrats, or reformed communists, launched his campaign in a popular city cafe after which he boarded a blue van for a tour of the country.
Tudjman's election campaign will officially start later on Wednesday.
Tomac and Gotovac were the only candidates who managed to secure enough support from voters to qualify for the presidential election -- each needed 10,000 signatures.

But neither seems to stand a chance of dethroning Tudjman who led Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia, and whose stature and authority within both his ruling HDZ party and the general population have grown ever since.
The president's aides have repeatedly said they expect him to win in the first round with more than 50 percent of votes.

Both Gotovac and Tomac vowed to change, if elected, the current system in which they argue the president has too much power over the government and parliament and to review the laws governing privatisation.

The 75-year old Tudjman, reportedly ill with cancer, has often been criticised for authoritarian rule and too tight a grip on all spheres of life, including the media. Critics also note the lavish lifestyle.
"Croatia should not have an elite power, living in high style," Tomac said, adding he would cut the presidential paraphernalia and entourage to a minimum.

"Social Democrats want to preserve private property and free entreprise, but we want to create a country which will protect the worker and his dignity, a country that will not allow a reign of furious capitalism," Tomac said.
He said he would give his support to Gotovac if he qualified for a second round.
"My goal is to offer a clear alternative -- and I think this is Gotovac's aim too...so if he gets to the second round he will have my support," Tomac said.
